title: Why Crocodiles Survived the Asteroid That Killed T. rex. #1 Is New
description: An asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago, but crocodiles kept swimming. Here are 5 survival secrets, from a year without food to alligators frozen in ice. Number one was published this month: crocs have chased warm climates for 245 million years. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: An asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs. So why are crocodiles still here?

scenes.label: 66 million years ago
scenes.say: Sixty-six million years ago, a space rock slammed into Earth. About three quarters of all species vanished.

scenes.label: Dinosaurs: gone
scenes.say: T. rex? Gone. Every giant dinosaur? Gone. Only their bird descendants made it through.

scenes.label: Stay for #1
scenes.say: But crocodiles just kept swimming. And this month, scientists finally figured out the biggest reason why. That one waits at the very end.

scenes.label: 5 secrets
scenes.say: Okay, so here's the plan. Five survival secrets, from weird to almost impossible. Each one stranger than the last.
And first, a quick question for you. Do you think crocodiles are older than dinosaurs? Keep your answer in mind.

scenes.label: 240+ million years
scenes.say: Because their family line, called Pseudosuchia, first appeared more than two hundred forty million years ago. Before the first dinosaurs.

scenes.label: Up to 12 m
scenes.say: And back then they weren't all swamp lurkers. Deinosuchus grew up to twelve meters long. It may have rivaled T. rex in mass.

scenes.label: Every kind of job
scenes.say: Some relatives ate plants. One was a filter feeder. Some lived out in the open ocean. One scientist said they filled almost every role imaginable.
So how did this ancient family dodge the worst day in Earth's history? Let's count it down.

scenes.label: Not all survived
scenes.say: Here's the thing, though. Lots of crocodile relatives did die out over time. The giants, the ocean hunters, the plant eaters. So surviving was never guaranteed.

scenes.label: Barely eats
scenes.say: Number five. They barely need to eat. And that's a superpower when the whole world runs out of food.

scenes.label: Solar powered
scenes.say: Crocodiles are cold-blooded. They warm up using the sun instead of burning food to make heat.
Think about that. A warm-blooded lion or bird has to burn food all day just to stay warm. A crocodile lets the sunshine do it for free.

scenes.label: About 50 meals a year
scenes.say: An average croc eats about fifty full meals a year. That's roughly one big meal a week.

scenes.label: 1 year, no food
scenes.say: And large crocodiles can go more than a year without a single meal. In extreme cases, they survive by using up their own body tissue.
Now picture the asteroid winter. Dust blocks the sun. Plants die. Then the plant eaters starve.
Big warm-blooded hunters needed tons of food, constantly. And some dinosaurs, maybe even T. rex, were warm-blooded.
A crocodile could just wait. Sit still, spend almost nothing, and outlast the famine. But here's the twist.

scenes.label: Strongest stomach acid
scenes.say: When a croc does eat, almost nothing goes to waste. Its stomach acid is the most acidic of any animal with a backbone.
It can digest bones, horns, hooves and even shells. In a starving world, anything becomes dinner.

scenes.label: Low power mode
scenes.say: Number four. They can turn their own bodies almost off. Like a phone on low power mode.

scenes.label: 2-3 beats a minute
scenes.say: A big saltwater crocodile can stay underwater for at least an hour. How? It slows its heart down to just two or three beats a minute.
Now feel your own pulse for a second. Imagine it slowing to just two beats a minute.

scenes.label: 4-chambered heart
scenes.say: And crocodilians are the only reptiles with a four-chambered heart. Just like ours. But with a secret hole.

scenes.label: Foramen of Panizza
scenes.say: That hole is called the foramen of Panizza. It lets blood mix between two main arteries, and keeps oxygen levels steady on long dives.
Their bodies can even send oxygen-rich blood mostly to the brain and heart, and less to everything else.

scenes.label: Aestivation
scenes.say: But it goes further. When it's too hot or dry, crocodilians can go dormant. That's called aestivation.

scenes.label: Sealed in mud
scenes.say: Some dig burrows. Others seal themselves inside hardened mud. Their heartbeat and breathing slow way down.
The study's lead scientist said that after the impact, cutting energy use like this was likely very advantageous.

scenes.label: Brumation
scenes.say: And if it gets too cold? They have a mode for that too. It's called brumation. And it looks completely unreal.

scenes.label: Frozen in ice
scenes.say: Number three. Alligators can survive frozen into ice. With just their noses poking out.

scenes.label: North Carolina
scenes.say: This happened at the Shallotte River Swamp Park in North Carolina. A cold snap froze the whole swamp solid.

scenes.label: Snout snorkel
scenes.say: And the alligators? Stuck in the ice, snouts sticking straight up into the air. Breathing.
They sensed the temperature dropping, and pushed their noses up before the surface froze. Smart, right?

scenes.label: 4°C water
scenes.say: Alligators can handle water as cold as four degrees Celsius. That's about forty Fahrenheit.

scenes.label: About a week
scenes.say: The park manager said they're still alive, still moving, but very lethargic. He guessed they could last about a week like that.
Then the air warmed to sixty-five Fahrenheit, the ice melted, and they just swam away.
An expert called it the opposite of what most crocodilians do. Normally, when it gets cold, they climb out and bask.
So now imagine a dark, cold impact winter. An animal that can slow down, wait, and breathe through ice? That's a survivor.
But slowing down isn't enough if you live in the wrong place. Which brings us to the water.

scenes.label: The safe zone
scenes.say: Number two. They lived in rivers and swamps. And fresh water might have been the safest place on Earth that day.

scenes.label: Top 0.5 cm
scenes.say: The heat from the blast is estimated to have evaporated only the top half centimeter of water. Deeper down, temperatures barely changed.
Fresh water life was already used to freezing winters and low oxygen. So the shock was something they'd practiced for.
Fast rivers could bring in fresh oxygen. Underground springs could keep some waters warm, and carry in bits of food from the land.

scenes.label: 6 months to 2 years
scenes.say: Scientists estimate the impact winter lasted somewhere between six months and two years. You just had to last that long.

scenes.label: Small, wet, not picky
scenes.say: And the surviving crocodilians had more going for them. Small bodies, a life half in water, and a diet of almost anything.

scenes.label: Only 25 species
scenes.say: There's a weird bonus too. Crocodiles look almost the same as they did around two hundred million years ago. Only twenty-five species live today.
Bristol scientists say crocs evolve very slowly, then speed up when the climate changes. Their body plan just worked.
Okay. Low power mode, ice snorkels, safe water. But none of that matters without the secret scientists published just this month.

scenes.label: Chasing heat
scenes.say: Number one. For two hundred forty-five million years, crocodiles have been chasing the heat. And it saved them.

scenes.label: 7,000+ fossils
scenes.say: A team at University College London mapped more than four hundred living and extinct species, using over seven thousand fossils.

scenes.label: 130,000 records
scenes.say: They added a hundred thirty thousand records of living crocodylians, and climate simulations stretching back two hundred forty-five million years.

scenes.label: 26-30°C
scenes.say: Their ancient comfort zone was about twenty-three degrees Celsius. Today's crocs prefer twenty-six to thirty.
Dinosaurs and mammals adapted to all kinds of climates. Crocodiles mostly didn't. They moved instead.

scenes.label: Crocs in Antarctica
scenes.say: When Earth warmed, they spread toward the poles. Around fifty million years ago, crocodile relatives lived as far as Antarctica.
When Earth cooled, they slid back toward the equator. Back and forth, for hundreds of millions of years.

scenes.label: Simulated impact
scenes.say: So the team ran the asteroid disaster through their climate models. Dimmed sunlight. Ash. Volcanic gas.

scenes.label: Warm refuges
scenes.say: And in nearly every scenario, warm pockets survived near the equator and the subtropics. Little hideouts where crocs could hang on.

scenes.label: 15% less sunlight
scenes.say: Only the most extreme case, a fifteen percent drop in sunlight, erased their climate everywhere. Dinosaur habitat collapsed in similar tests.
So crocodiles didn't win by being the toughest. They won by staying in the warm spots. Here's the twist, though.

scenes.label: Room to move
scenes.say: The researchers warn that today's crocodiles survive climate change by moving. So as the planet warms, they'll need room to move.
And in a world full of farms and cities, finding that room might not be easy.
Think about that. The trick that beat an asteroid only works if there's somewhere warm to go. Habitat is everything.
So, were you right? Crocodiles came before the dinosaurs, and they outlived them.

scenes.label: Your pick?
scenes.say: Which survival secret blew your mind most? The year without food, the ice snorkel, or chasing the heat? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: How Crocodiles Survived the Asteroid That Killed T. rex
short.description: Crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A new Science Advances study shows they always chased warm climates. Full countdown of 5 survival secrets on my channel.

scenes.say: Crocodiles survived the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs, and now we know why.
Sixty-six million years ago, about three quarters of all species vanished. T. rex was gone.
But crocodiles barely need food. Big ones can go more than a year without a meal.
They can slow their heart to two or three beats a minute. Alligators even survive frozen in ice, noses poking out.
And a new study of over seven thousand fossils shows crocs always chased the heat. Toward the poles when warm, the equator when cold.
In nearly every asteroid simulation, warm hideouts survived near the equator. Dinosaur habitat collapsed.
So they just stayed warm and waited. That's how crocodiles survived the asteroid that killed the dinosaurs, and now we know why.
